title: Syllabus
text:
Assessments in brief
Weekly exercises are released before class on Wednesdays in Weeks 1–12 and due 11:59 PM the following Wednesday. They are distributed and submitted through GitHub; an autograder reports which questions pass every time you push, and you may resubmit freely before the deadline. Late: 20% penalty within 24h, 40% within 48h, zero after that.
In-class quizzes (15 minutes, five total: Weeks 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) are paper-based hand-fluency checks completed individually without laptops, phones, or AI assistance during the last 20 minutes of class. To provide flexibility for unexpected illness or travel, your lowest quiz score is automatically dropped (the best 4 of 5 count, 3.75% each, 15% total).
The final project is an individual analysis of a public-health dataset: a reproducible Quarto report in a GitHub repository, a 5-minute recorded video walkthrough, and an AI-use appendix. Released Week 10, due 11:59 PM December 16. No late submissions.

title: Statistical Programming in R
text:
Wednesdays 2:00–4:40 PM · 70 Washington Sq S (Bobst), Room LL138 · Sep 2 – Dec 9, 2026 (no class Oct 14)
Welcome! This course teaches R programming for the full data-analysis workflow: wrangling, visualization, simulation, and reproducible reporting with Quarto, using public-health data throughout. You will also learn two skills that now define professional statistical programming: managing code with Git and GitHub, and using AI coding assistants responsibly (prompting, verifying, and debugging AI-generated code).
No prior programming or statistics experience is required.

title: Statistical Programming in R
text:
How the course works

Hands-on classes. Every session alternates short live-coding demos with paired exercises, so you write code in every class.
Instant feedback. Weekly exercises are submitted on GitHub and checked automatically: push your work, see which questions pass, revise, and resubmit until the deadline.
AI, embraced and verified. AI tools are allowed on homework and the project (with disclosure), taught explicitly in Week 8, and set aside during short in-class quizzes where your own fluency is certified.
One real project. The course builds to an individual analysis of a public-health dataset: a reproducible Quarto report, a GitHub repo, and a 5-minute video walkthrough.

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Why Statistical Programming in R?


Why R?

Public Health Standard: CDC, WHO, FDA, academic journals, and health agencies run on R.
Tidyverse Ecosystem: Unmatched tools for data wrangling (dplyr), visualization (ggplot2), and modeling.
Open & Reproducible: Free, community-driven, transparent science.


Why This Course?

No prior programming required.
Full data pipeline: Import \(\rightarrow\) Clean \(\rightarrow\) Visualize \(\rightarrow\) Simulate \(\rightarrow\) Report.
Modern professional toolkit: Quarto + Git/GitHub + Responsible AI assistance.

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
The Modern Data Science Stack
In this course, you will master four core technologies:

R: The statistical computing engine.
RStudio: The integrated development environment (IDE).
Quarto (.qmd): Reproducible scientific publishing (replaces Word/PDF/slides).
Git & GitHub: Version control, collaboration, and automated grading.
AI Assistants: Prompting, verifying, and debugging code with LLMs.

We do not do passive lectures. Each class is split into interactive cycles:

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
R as an Interactive Calculator
You type commands into the Console; R evaluates them and prints results.
# Arithmetic
12 + 35
(100 - 32) * 5 / 9   # Fahrenheit to Celsius

# Math functions
sqrt(64)
exp(1)
log(10)              # Natural logarithm (base e)
log10(100)           # Common logarithm (base 10)






Tip


Everything after # is a comment and is ignored by R. Use comments to document your thinking!

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Objects and Variable Assignment
We store values in named objects using the assignment operator <- (Alt + - or Option + -):
# Assigning a value
participant_age <- 28
height_m <- 1.75
weight_kg <- 68.5

# Using objects in expressions
bmi <- weight_kg / (height_m^2)
bmi

Names must start with a letter and can contain letters, numbers, _, and ..
R is case-sensitive (bmi \(\neq\) BMI).

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Functions and Getting Help
Functions take arguments (inputs) and return an output:
# Rounding
round(bmi, digits = 1)

# Summary statistics
vals <- c(10, 20, 30, NA)
mean(vals, na.rm = TRUE)
Getting help in R:

?round or help(round) — opens the official documentation.
example(round) — runs examples from the help page.

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Packages & The Course Textbook: R02Pro
R packages extend R with datasets and specialized functions.
# Install once per computer (done in Console, not script):
install.packages("r02pro")

# Load in every session where you need it:
library(r02pro)

Textbook: R Programming: Zero to Pro (Free online: r02pro.github.io).

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Why Quarto?


❌ The Traditional Way

Run code in R \(\rightarrow\) Copy table to Excel \(\rightarrow\) Paste into Word \(\rightarrow\) Export PDF.
Data changes? Repeat everything manually and risk copy-paste errors!


✅ The Quarto Way
One reproducible .qmd document combining:

Narrative text (Markdown)
Executable code (R chunks)
Dynamic tables & plots compiled directly on demand.

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Anatomy of a Quarto Document (.qmd)
A .qmd document combines three elements:


1. YAML Metadata (Header):
---
title: "My Analysis"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
---
2. Markdown Narrative (Text):
## Introduction
Here is text with **bold** & *italics*.

3. Code Chunks (Live Computation):
# An R code chunk
mean_age <- mean(c(25, 30, 45))
mean_age
\(\longrightarrow\) Click Render (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K) to compile directly into a polished HTML report!

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Markdown Text Formatting Cheat Sheet



Syntax
Rendered Output




# Heading 1
Largest Section Header


## Heading 2
Sub-section Header


**bold text**
bold text


*italic text*
italic text


- item 1
Bulleted list


1. item 1
Numbered list


$E = mc^2$
Inline math: \(E = mc^2\)

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Code Chunk Options
Control how code executes and displays using #|:
#| echo: true       # Show code in final report (default)
#| eval: true       # Run code (default)
#| warning: false   # Suppress package warnings
#| message: false   # Suppress package startup messages
#| fig-width: 7     # Control plot width
Click the Render button (or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K) in RStudio to generate your HTML report!

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Why Version Control?


❌ The File Chaos (Without Git)

report_v1.docx
report_v2.docx
report_v2_edit.docx
report_final_REALLY_FINAL.docx
😱 Which file has the correct numbers?


✅ The Git Way

Recorded history: Every change is a snapshot with a commit message.
Safe experiments: Try new ideas on branches without breaking main code.
Seamless team collaboration: No emailed zip files or overwritten work.

🔴 Zone 2: Quizzes

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
AI Corner: The “Verify-Then-Use” Rule


❌ The Bad AI User

Prompts: “Do my homework question 3.”
Copies and pastes code blindly.
Submits hallucinated functions or incorrect math without understanding.


✅ The Statistical Programmer

Prompts: “How do I compute the trimmed mean in R while handling NAs?”
Inspects the output against R documentation.
Tests edge cases.
Owns and understands every line.

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
The Four Atomic Vector Types
In R, every element in an atomic vector must have the same type:


1. Numeric (Double)
Decimal numbers (default in R):
weights <- c(68.5, 72.0, 81.3)
typeof(weights) # "double"
2. Integer
Explicit whole numbers with L:
counts <- c(1L, 5L, 12L)
typeof(counts)  # "integer"

3. Character (Strings)
Text enclosed in quotes:
drugs <- c("aspirin", "statin", "placebo")
typeof(drugs)   # "character"
4. Logical (Booleans)
TRUE or FALSE (all caps):
adherent <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
typeof(adherent)# "logical"

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
The Type Hierarchy & Implicit Coercion
What happens when you mix different types in c(...)?
R silently converts everything to the least restrictive type:
\[\text{logical} \longrightarrow \text{integer} \longrightarrow \text{double} \longrightarrow \text{character}\]
# Logical to numeric (TRUE becomes 1, FALSE becomes 0)
sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE))  # Count how many TRUEs: 3
mean(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE))# Proportion of TRUEs: 0.5

# Numeric + Character becomes Character
c(10, 25, "missing")             # c("10", "25", "missing")






Pro-Tip for Health Data


mean(bp > 140, na.rm = TRUE) directly calculates the prevalence of hypertension by coercing logicals to 1s and 0s!

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Summary Statistics on Vectors
R has built-in vector aggregators:
chol <- c(185, 220, 240, 195, 210, NA)

length(chol)              # Total elements including NA (6)
sum(is.na(chol))          # Count missing values (1)
mean(chol, na.rm = TRUE)  # Arithmetic mean (212)
sd(chol, na.rm = TRUE)    # Standard deviation (20.8)
summary(chol)             # 5-number summary + Mean + NAs

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Sequences with : and seq()
Instead of typing numbers manually, generate sequences automatically:


The Colon Operator :
Consecutive integer sequences:
1:10
20:15    # Counts backward!
-3:3

The seq() Function
Flexible step sizes & lengths:
# By step size
seq(from = 0, to = 100, by = 20)
# Output: 0 20 40 60 80 100

# By total length
seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 5)
# Output: 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Repetition with rep()
The rep() function replicates values using times or each:


times (Pattern repetition)
Repeats the whole vector:
rep(c("A", "B"), times = 3)
# "A" "B" "A" "B" "A" "B"

# Unequal repetitions per element:
rep(c("Control", "Treated"), times = c(4, 2))
# "Control" "Control" "Control" "Control" "Treated" "Treated"

each (Element repetition)
Repeats each item before moving to next:
rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3)
# "A" "A" "A" "B" "B" "B"

# Combining both:
rep(c("Dose1", "Dose2"), each = 2, times = 2)
# "Dose1" "Dose1" "Dose2" "Dose2" "Dose1" "Dose1" "Dose2" "Dose2"

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Modulo Arithmetic %%
The modulo operator %% calculates the remainder of division:
14 %% 3   # 2  (14 = 4 * 3 + 2)
10 %% 2   # 0  (10 is even)






Common Applications in Data Science



Even numbers: x %% 2 == 0
Divisible by 5: x %% 5 == 0
Assigning participants to \(K\) rotating study groups: (1:N) %% K + 1

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
The Three Subsetting Methods
We extract elements using square brackets x[...]:
ages <- c(23, 45, 19, 31, 56, 42)


1. Positive Indices
Extract by position (1-indexed):
ages[1]        # 23
ages[c(1, 4)]  # 23 31
ages[2:4]      # 45 19 31

2. Negative Indices
Exclude specific positions:
ages[-1]       # All except 1st
ages[-c(2, 5)] # Drop 2nd & 5th
# ages[-2:4]   # ERROR! Use -(2:4)

3. Logical Subsetting
Extract where TRUE:
ages[ages > 40]
# 45 56 42

ages[ages >= 30 & ages <= 50]
# 45 31 42

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Logical Operators for Filtering
Combine conditions using element-wise logical operators:








Operator
Meaning
Example




&
Element-wise AND (both true)
(bmi > 25) & (age > 50)


\|
Element-wise OR (either true)
(status == "Severe") \| (fever == TRUE)


!
Logical NOT (inversion)
!(city %in% c("NY", "CA"))


%in%
Value matching (set membership)
id %in% confirmed_cases



sbp <- c(118, 142, 135, 160, 122)
stage2_htn <- sbp >= 140
sbp[stage2_htn]   # 142 160

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Modifying Vectors in Place (Mutation)
Use subsetting on the left side of <- to update specific elements:
scores <- c(88, -99, 95, -99, 72)

# Replace survey code -99 with NA:
scores[scores == -99] <- NA
scores
# 88 NA 95 NA 72

# Cap values at 90 (winsorizing):
scores[scores > 90 & !is.na(scores)] <- 90
scores
# 88 NA 90 NA 72

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Sorting, Ranking, and Ordering
Understanding the difference between sort(), rank(), and order():
vals <- c(30, 10, 50, 20)


sort(x)
Returns sorted values:
sort(vals)
# 10 20 30 50

sort(vals, decreasing = TRUE)
# 50 30 20 10

rank(x)
Returns rank position of each element:
rank(vals)
# 3 1 4 2
# (30 is 3rd, 10 is 1st, etc.)

order(x)
Returns indices that would sort x:
order(vals)
# 2 4 1 3
vals[order(vals)] # sorted!

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Handling Ties in rank()
When numbers repeat, how should ranks be assigned?
scores <- c(80, 95, 80, 70)

rank(scores)                        # Default: average ranks (2.5 4.0 2.5 1.0)
rank(scores, ties.method = "first") # By appearance: (2 4 3 1)
rank(scores, ties.method = "min")   # Sports ranking: (2 4 2 1)






Tip


ties.method = "first" is essential for deterministic top-\(K\) rankings in data pipelines!

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
AI Corner: Beware Vector Recycling!
When R operates on vectors of different lengths, it silently recycles the shorter one:


What R Does:
x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
y <- c(1, 2)
x + y
# Computes: 10+1, 20+2, 30+1, 40+2
# Output: 11 22 31 42

⚠️ The Danger with AI:

LLMs often generate code that accidentally recycles vectors when filtering or standardizing.
Always check length(x) == length(y) before element-wise operations!

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text: This course treats AI coding assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and similar) as professional tools: you will learn to use them effectively and critically, and you will also develop the individual fluency to program without them.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text:
Why this policy
Statistical programmers now work alongside AI tools daily. Banning them would prepare you for a world that no longer exists; letting them do your thinking would leave you unable to catch their mistakes, and they make plenty. The course therefore teaches the skill that actually matters: directing AI tools and verifying their output. Week 8 is a dedicated workshop, and every week includes a short “AI corner” showing one good and one bad AI use for that week’s topic.
Free-tier AI tools are sufficient for all coursework; no paid subscriptions are required or expected.
Submitting AI-generated work you do not understand, using AI during a quiz, or omitting required disclosure is an academic-integrity violation.
